en: The Sūtra on the Iron City Hell,
translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Tanwulan of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
At a time when the Buddha was at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Śrāvastī, the Buddha exhorted the śramaṇas.
The Gatekeeper said:

"With my divine eye, I behold all people in the world—their births and deaths, their beauty and ugliness, their nobility and lowliness; those who, upon death, attain the good path and those who attain the evil path. Those who, while in the world, commit evil with their bodies, speak evil with their mouths, and harbor evil thoughts in their hearts, and who constantly delight in cooking and killing to sacrifice to ghosts and spirits, shall enter the hells (*niraya*) when their bodies die.
Those who always practice goodness with their bodies, always speak goodness with their mouths, and always harbor goodness in their hearts, ascend to heaven upon death."
The Buddha said:

"Human beings are like bubbles in the rain; as the rain falls from above, for every bubble that breaks, another bubble forms. When humans are born into this world, those who are born and those who die are like the mere rising of bubbles."

The Buddha, wielding the divine eye, beholds all people in the world: those who die to ascend to heaven and those who enter niraya; the poor and the wealthy, the noble and the lowly, and the good and evil deeds performed by each person.
The Buddha said:
"I know them all. It is like this:

suppose at night, on both sides of a city gate, two torches are lit. If there are several million people passing through, whether entering or exiting, one looking from the darkness will see all those entering and exiting within the light of the fires."
The Buddha said:

"With my divine eye I observe the people of the world: some, upon death, ascend to heaven; others enter niraya (hell). It is like a person looking from the darkness at those entering and exiting a fire, or like one atop a high tower looking down upon several thousand households; from above, one sees all the houses clearly."
The Buddha said:
"I see those among the people of the world who, upon death, ascend to heaven or enter the hells, just as a person from atop a high tower looks down upon various households."
The Buddha said:
"It is like a person traveling by boat through clear water, seeing all the fish and stones within the water.

When the Buddha uses his divine eye to observe the people of the world—those who, after death, ascend to heaven and those who enter the hells—it is as if that person were looking at the fish and stones in clear water."
There is a bright moon pearl; when one threads it with five-colored silks and people look at the pearl, they all see the five colors and can distinguish that they are strung through the pearl.
The Buddha said:
"I see the origins of the good and evil transformations of the people in the world as clearly as a person looking at this pearl."
The Buddha said:

“I see those people in the world who are unfilial toward their parents, who do not serve śramaṇas or practitioners, who do not respect their elders, who do not fear the prohibitions of the authorities, and who have no dread of this life or the next—they are neither startled nor terrified.”
When such people die, they immediately enter hell and meet King Yama; thus they depart from good and return to evil.
The executioners of hell are called *pang*; these *pang* then lead the person forward to the presence of King Yama.
The henchmen of Niraya said:

"When this person was a human being in the world, he was unfilial toward his parents, did not serve śramaṇas or practitioners of the Way, did not respect his elders, did not practice giving, feared neither this world nor the next, and had no dread of the local officials."
"Yama shall judge this person's transgressions and sins.
Then Yama called the person forward and addressed him before Yama, saying:

"When you were a human being in the world, your parents nurtured you, pushing aside the dry bedding to give you the moist, nursing you with their milk until you grew large. Why were you not filial toward your parents?"
The person then replied to Yama:
"I was indeed foolish and arrogant. Yama said:

"Regarding those who dwell in their transgressions: it is not the fault of parents, nor of heaven, nor of emperors, nor of śramaṇas or practitioners; what you have done with your own bodies, you must receive for yourselves. This is the first question."
The second question:
"Do you not see that when one is afflicted by severe illness and extreme weakness, the hands and feet become utterly incapable of functioning?
That person replied:
"I truly saw it. Yama said, "Why did you not reform yourself and do good?"
The person replied,
"I was indeed foolish and arrogant. Yama said:
"This fault is not the work of the heavens, nor of one's parents, nor of a sovereign, nor of śramaṇas or practitioners; it is what you yourself have done, and you must experience its consequences."
Yama asked a third time:

"Do you not see that when men and women in this world reach old age, their eyes can no longer see and their ears can no longer hear; they must walk leaning on staffs, and their black hair turns white, so that they are no longer like they were in their youth?"
The man said, "I truly saw an old man walking along,
leaning on a staff. Yama said:
"At this time, why did you not reform yourself and do good?
The man replied, "I was truly foolish and arrogant."

Yama said: "This fault is not the fault of your parents, nor of the heavens, nor of the sovereign, nor of śramaṇas or practitioners; it is what you yourself have done, and you must experience its consequences."
Yama asked a fourth question:

"In your time in the world, did you not see men and women who, after one day, two days, up to seven days had passed since their death, had their bodies rotting and their forms ruined, being devoured by worms and ants, and loathed by all people?"
"Having seen this, why do you not reform yourself and become good?
The man replied, "I have indeed seen it; I was truly foolish and arrogant."

Yama said: "As for your conduct, why did you not rectify your mind, rectify your speech, and rectify your actions? This fault is not the fault of your parents, nor of the heavens, nor of the sovereign, nor the fault of śramaṇas or practitioners; it is what you yourself have done, and you must receive its consequences."
Yama’s fifth question:

“When you were a human being, did you ever see in this world officials who had captured robbers, murderers, or thieves, and bound them back-to-back to send them to prison for interrogation and punishment; or did you see them led out of the city and beaten to death along the road; or did you see some who were executed alive by being stretched upon a rack? Did you see such things?”
The man said, "I truly saw it. Yama said:
"Why do you not practice giving and perform wholesome deeds?
When you were a human being, why did you not rectify your conduct, rectify your speech, and rectify your mind?
The person replied:
"You were truly foolish and arrogant," said Yama.

"This fault was not caused by your parents, nor by the heavens, nor by the sovereign, nor by śramaṇas or practitioners of the Way; it was what you yourself did, and you must receive the consequences thereof."
Once the interrogation was finished, the wardens of hell immediately seized and led him away, taking him to an iron city;

this is the first hell. The city of the Avīci Hell has four gates and is four thousand li in circumference. Within it is a great cauldron forty li long. The wardens impale the person with forks and thrust them inside. Thus, within countless such vessels there is fire; seeing them from afar, all people are struck with terror and tremble.

In this manner, tens of millions of people enter; they are cast into the margins of the niraya hells and cannot emerge day or night. All the gates are closed and do not open, so they cannot get out. People remain within for tens of millions of years, yet the fire does not go out and the people do not die.
After a long time, they saw from afar that the eastern gate opened of its own accord, and everyone ran toward it wishing to exit.
Just as they reached the gate, it closed again; those who wished to leave then began to fight and quarrel with one another at the gate, desiring to get out.
After a long time, he again saw from afar the western gate open; everyone ran toward it, but the gate closed again, and the people once more began to fight together at the gate.
After a long time, he again saw the southern gate open; everyone ran toward it, but the gate closed again, and the people once more began to fight together at the gate.
After a long time, the four gates open again, and the person emerges, believing they have been liberated; yet they enter the second *kauya* hell once more.
When their feet touch the ground, they are instantly scorched, but when they lift them, the flesh grows back again.

Some run to the east, some to the west, some to the south, and some to the north; the ground all around becomes intensely hot, and after many tens of millions of years, it finally ends, whereupon they imagine they have escaped.
Furthermore, they enter the third hell, Mili-ma-dre-ni-li. Within it there are insects called "Tortoise-beak" (Kukṣi); their snouts are like iron, and their heads and feet are black.

When these insects see people from afar, they all come forward to peck at them until their flesh and bones are completely consumed. This continues for many tens of millions of years before it finally ends.
Thinking they have escaped, they enter again the fourth hell, Cullamala.

Within it there is a mountain with rocks as sharp as knives; people all run to its summit, while others run down from it, all seeking liberation. Unaware of their direction, their feet are sliced and flayed; the ground stones are all like sharp blades. Thus they endure for many tens of millions of years until it finally ends.
Thinking he has escaped, the person enters again into the fifth hell, Āvīcī-khaṇḍa. Within it there is a hot wind;

wherever they encounter it, they seek to avoid it but cannot escape. That person wishes for death but cannot die, and wishes for life but cannot live; thus, after a long time of many tens of millions of years, they finally emerge.

Believing he has escaped, the person enters again the sixth hell, Aṭaṭa (the Hell of Shivering), where there are many trees all covered in thorns. Between the trees dwell demons; when a person enters therein, fire issues from the demons' heads and fire issues from their mouths. Their bodies consist of sixteen thorns. Seeing the person approaching from afar, they become enraged, and the fire reveals those sixteen thorns, which pierce the person's body until it is split asunder as if being devoured. The person runs in every direction, seeking to escape, yet constantly encounters these demons in this manner for tens of millions of years before finally emerging.
The person thinks they have escaped, but they enter again into the seventh hell, Paṃsuvālukā-niraya.

Within it there are insects; these insects are named *śūna*. When a person enters therein, these insects fly into their mouths and devour their bodies. The people run to the utmost limit, yet the insects devour them without ceasing. They run in all four directions, seeking escape, but cannot find it. In this manner, after many tens of millions of years, they finally emerge.
Believing they have escaped, the people enter again the eighth hell, the *Tāṇḍanīyū* (or *Tāṇḍana*) hell.

Within it there is flowing water; all the people fall into the water. Beside the water are thorny brambles, and the heat of the water exceeds that of the cauldrons of the world. It boils and surges so fiercely that everyone is cooked and disintegrated. As they run seeking to reach the bank, demons holding pitchforks impale them from behind through their bellies. Unable to escape, they all follow the current downstream.
Furthermore, there were ghosts who seized them with hooks as if prodding them, asking:
"From where have you come? Why do you ask this?"
The man said: "I do not know from where I have come, nor do I know where I shall go;
I am merely hungry and thirsty, and wish to pursue food and drink."
The ghost said, "I will give you food.

He immediately took up a hook and hooked its upper and lower jaws, causing the mouth to gape wide open; he then poured molten copper into the person's mouth, which caused it to burn and fester. Thus, though seeking death, they could not die; though seeking life, they could not live.
Because that person had committed such extreme evils during their lifetime while living as a human in the world, they sought liberation but could not attain it.
Although those in the various hells all managed to escape, thinking they had attained deliverance, they instead entered the seventh hell.
The ghost asked in opposition:

"You went away; why have you returned to enter the fifth, returned again to enter the fourth, from the fourth returned again to enter the third, returned again to enter the second, and returned again to enter the first, the Avīci Mahānaraka?"
Before they had arrived, the people saw the iron city from afar; they all rejoiced, shouting loudly and crying "Ten Thousand Years!
When Yama heard this, he immediately questioned the attendants of the hells:
"What kind of sound is this?"
The bystander immediately said,
"This voice is that of one who previously passed through the hells. Yama said:

"These are all those who are unfilial toward their parents, who fear neither Heaven nor the sovereign, who do not serve śramaṇas or practitioners of the Way, and who do not dread the prohibitive precepts."
Yama then called the person forward again and addressed him, saying:

"If you do not fear the words of Yama, and if you now depart in liberation, yet shall become a son to human beings once more, you must serve your elders with filial piety; you must stand in awe of the prohibitions and precepts of the sovereign; you must attend upon śramaṇas and practitioners, rectifying your mind, your speech, and your body."
While one is alive in this world, transgressions are small and light; once dead beneath the earth, the hells (niraya) are vast and heavy.
If one attains the state of a śramaṇa or a practitioner of the Way, they should serve that path; if they attain arhatship, all paths to the hells will be closed off.

"When each pair has finished [their turn], all those within the hells are able to emerge. Once outside the city walls, they all die again; as for these deceased ones, according to their past karma from former lives—when they were humans—they committed evil but still possessed some small measure of goodness. Having returned from the hells, they are all reborn in the good realms."
When people emerge from the hells, each governs their own mind, speech, and conduct, and they no longer return to enter the hells.
The hells do not call out to people; rather, as people undergo the foul, poisonous, and painful suffering of the hells, they each reflect for themselves that they ought to practice virtue.
The Buddha said:
"When a person dies and enters Niraya, only kings, marquises, śramaṇas, and practitioners may meet with Yama; all other ordinary people merely enter following the crowd."
"Yama is the name of the King of Hell.
— *The Sūtra on the Iron City Niraya Spoken by the Buddha*
